words: Some people are afraid of flying; you're not afraid?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I have a great grandson who just left to go back to Colorado Springs, and he's a flyer. He just got his license to teach others. And, they were here three weeks. And they went back; he's got another year, then he'll be through. Now I have another one that is a captain in the Air Force in Germany, and he has been released. And, he is on his way home.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Will he come and see you then?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh, yes. Yes, he will; pretty quick after he arrives.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, tell me some more of the skills, some more of the things you like to do, or that you used to like to do.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, as I say,, ~cooking . ..

speaker: Connie Richard
words: ... was your favorite thing ...

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: ... of all things, and I've held down some big jobs.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Have you? Tell me about those.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: When I was sixty-two, I'm eighty-seven, when I was sixty-two I had a, well, it was a probably average of forty men, loggers.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: And you cooked for them?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Of course, I had some help, but I ioyed every minute of it.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Did you have any other kinds of jobs?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, during the period of years if I was not doing anything, I went out nursing quite a bit. I wasn't a nurse ...

speaker: Connie Richard
words: But you knew about it ...

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I knew quite a bit.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Did you ever help people deliver babies or anything?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, I never did. I have been in surgery with a couple of people.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You have? In a home?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, in the hospital; older people, nervous and wouldn't go in to be operated on, and I have seen two operations.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Did you like that or not?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, I kind of seen the inside of everything . . . different that the outside.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Any other kinds of things that you did?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, not in particular.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Do you like reading or sewing knitting, or crocheting?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh, I love to read and I love to knit, but my eyes don't take it anymore.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Yeah, well you did before though.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, now I can't see good enough.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Do you have any other interests, or hobbies, or talents?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I don't think so, I wouldn't say anything is a talent.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Lots of things are talents; your cooking was a talent.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, yes i mean that, you know.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You never played an instrument or anything like that?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Piano.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Did you? See! Probably are lots of things; I have to pull them out of you, come on, you have to volunteer this information !

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I had a piano ... I sold it; I haven't anything.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Have you ever entered anything in 4-H Fairs or County Fairs or anything?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, I never did. I liked to cook and can, and glop the food up, that's why I'm so big, I guess.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You're not very big. Okay, did you ever belong to any clubs or groups or anything?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: About a month ago I received my little diamond, and I got a life-membership to the 'Stars' .

speaker: Connie Richard
words: What's the 'Stars'?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, it's suwused to be the biggest, best women's club. Yeah, fifty years. They gave me a big celebration, and I got the little pin, it's small, like that - a star with the diamonds. I'm awfully proud of that.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Yeah, that's nice. Well, what did that group do, what kind of an organization was it?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I don't know, do you belong to any lodge or ...

speaker: Connie Richard
words: No, that's why I don't know what it is.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, it's an organization and our work, of course I'm talking about the 'Stars' now, our work all comes from the Bible. Our work is unwritten.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Is it something like the 'Masons"?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: It's the women's organization of the 'Masons'.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Oh, I see.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: And, I have a life-membership; now on this membership I paid in what you call the "Home Fund'.' It is five dollars a year; I've paid in now for fifty years. So, if I would become broke, or have to have help, I could move into a home. I think our biggest home is in Southern California. But, I've got another home if I ever get kicked out of here!

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Have you been doing anything to get kicked out of here?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No. Oh, I get balled-out quite a bit.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: What for?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Smoking in the wrong spot! Someplace .. , they're awful nice to me, I have no kick. Only it does take alot of money, alot of it.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Do you consider yourself kind of a country girl or rural type.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yes.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: And do you like thinking of yourself that way?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yes, I like it that way.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: How come?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I don't know, of course as a young person, I didn't live in the city. I've been through to visit, but never to live there. And, I just acquired a ... that I prefer the country.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: What do you like about the country?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, room ••. you can get out and walk around without a thousand people staring at you; I just like it. And, of course, I used to, not any more - I'm too crippled I enjoyed going out on picnics, or camping a week-end or a week or so; I can recall many nice times I had with my mom and dad. Going out picking huckleberries, or something like that. No, I like the country. Really, when you stop to think about it, you go into a city, you see all the high, high buildings and they all look alike; to me they do.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: When you were married, can you tell me a little bit about your relationship with your husband, I mean, did he ever ask your advice on things?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I'll tell you, he was a very hard worker. I took care of the business.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You had a business with him?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: So it wasn't new to me when he away before at all.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Had you been keeping the books and managing it and everything?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, and then I had quite a little bit of property when he died.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: I've been finding out alot that alot of the women had helped manage and kept books for their husband's business; I guess it's just one way that rural women can help out.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, when there were big decisions to make like when he was a ranger and you were alone alot, then he was thoughtful of you I guess. Was that his main reason for quitting?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah because he ... at that time there were no roads, there was no tele phone; maybe a telephone, oh, thirty miles or something. And, of course, me living in that lodge alot just alone.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: So he was being thoughtful of you.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh, well, he was awfully good to me. I can't understand, you know, he was such an honest, decent person ... and yet he be like he was taken too soon, but we think back. Now there's one thing I don't want to forget before I cut loose from you - is about our flood.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Tell me about that.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, that flood was in '16 and '17, I mean, I don't know just what year, because it was at Christmas time. And, we were living up the river, oh, maybe ten miles up the river -we had a logging job - and the oldest boy, however, was older, he was seven and the youngest one was three years younger, And, quite alot of snow, and we were right on the bank of the river; in fact, we had a tent - oh it'd probably be twice as big as this room with a good floor in it and boards up quite a ways, and then the tent. And the boy had to walk about, oh, two miles to school. And, I don't know that morning when he left, it was raining, and yet there was snow. I was rather watchful and thoughtful that day, and he had to cross the river on a whip log and that wasn't easy, but then •.. water. And I had often, when I would know it was time for him to come home, I would delay just a little bit to see if he would attempt to walk it; he never did. But anyway, I walked across the logs and helped him over to the camp, and it rained; it seemed to me like it was water pouring all night. And, every once in a while I'd get up and look to see if the river was high as I thought it was - well it wouldn't be. But the next morning it started to come, and I had nin~ men, crew people, and always kept plenty of groceries, of course, and meat. In fact, that day I had a quarter of beef delivered. And, after being pulled out of here, we went to another camp. I walked four miles on the mountain. And I thought, "Thank God I got that quarter of beef." I was still thinking of feeding the men because the roads had washed out; the railroad · washed out! That's when the railroad washed out through Ederville, you know, upside-down. Well, anyway, I wasn't too restful that morning, but I fed the men at eleven o'clock. And, my land, all of a sudden the water began to come in and I began to put on clothes on the children - to keep them as warm and as dry as I could. I didn't think much of myself, but I got the kids dressed warm. By the time I got them ready, I had a long window like this above my worktable, and they had to break the window out, of course, they were in a hurry, and pull the kids and I out of the window. And, there was a low place, kind of a swampy affair, they had to fall a tree across that for the kids and I to walk to BENING/RICHARD 20 mountain. Then we had this four or five mile walk to another camp - they were up in the mountain higher. And we started off the walk, and the little fellow, of course he's a man now - thirty-two - he said the only thing he remembers about us leaving was me falling. And I fell with my head downhill! Well, my husband pulled and even the seven-year-old tried; I had an awful time trying to get out of an old bag car; they had logged it, you know, then piled it in the brush, and, of course, was soft and I can't see it. But anyway, I got over to the other camp, and the woman that was cooking there was big - I always was - and I could wear her clothes. But the kids, I had to take their clothes off and dry them before they had many to put on, although I had them well-dressed. Well we had to stay there three days before the water went down. I had a sky-light above my work• table - a window in the roof, you know - and there were three men went over to see what was going on. Of course, that window was open that we broke to get me out; the water was just on top of the table. So, anyway, well then we waited for it to go down and we hopped back! We all stayed over there; we had no place to go. And, of course, I was still a-fretting about food. Well, I had just bought a case of butter, the butter was filled, and I thought, "Oh, I've got that meat!" So I went out and got my quarter of beef and cut it, and I thought it felt funny - kind of gritty or something ••. we couldn't eat it .•. it was full of gravel! Well, then we didn't have any meat. But, I had flour - we had cloth sacks then - and, of course, the water was around it, but it formed a crust. I could reach down and get the flour, and we had bread; we didn't have much to eat. Oh, that broke us. I'll tell you, I know what it is to be awfully poor. We lost everything! Our shoot washed out, the roads washed out, we had nothing. (Friend): Took so much work to build it.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh, we were so poor.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: How long was it before you had money or supplies?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, of course, I had friends that sent clothes and things; you know, they knew about the size ... I wasn't fussy - just something to wrap around me! Oh, it took us quite a little while, then I took sick; I was miserable and trying to work and I couldn't. We had a little place in Edaville - little home, two bedrooms, and the kitchen, dining room and living room. The water was on top of the mattresses, and mud; and what few clothes I'd left there were destroyed. I know my rug was just mud like that; they took it up, though - some of the friends - and took it down to the river and let the water run through it. Finally, it got dry enough and clean enough that I had it cleaned, but it never looked the same. Oh, we were poor.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Now, was that during the depression too - was that depression time?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, no.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: What happened to you during the depression?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, we were very fortunate. My husband was timberchief of the Haccoff Mining Company; he never missed a payday. His wages were cut, but he never missed a payday.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: They still were able to pay him.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: And, of course, we helped alot of people. I know he always said, "Now listen, we' re awfully lucky. People especially with kids who have got to have food. Well, then for $10 I could buy quite alot of groceries. I sent out a good many $10 worth of groceries. Because people had been hungry! But, he never missed a payday.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Where were you living then during the depression?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh, lived in Wallace, had some property here and I kept it rented, and, of course, I had to pay rent there. But, we were lucky.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: And then, what about the First and Second World Wars; your husband wasn't involved with the wars?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, not at all. All we had done was work. In the last war, of course, we were out of Orofino up in the mountains, and I cooked all the time - we couldn't get help. And, I learned ... ! made up a lot of new recipes that if I were in my home now, I would still use them.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: What were they?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, one of them, I called it a Bean Loaf. I would boil the beans and get them quite tender, and then put them through a food-grinder and would mix, oh, take the cheap cuts of meat like pig's feet or something like that, and cook them and grind them and put them in there. And, oh,spices or whatever I wanted to add to it, and bake it and tried to aim to have broth sometimes to make gravy to put over it. It was awfully good!

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Sounds good. People need to know those recipes now, because food is so expensive.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yes! I don't know if people would try to do it. I'm so sorry for kids today - well, we were lucky.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, I guess everybody learns how to manage; you had real poor times, too, and everybody has to learn how to live through them.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I often think now what would happen if a real depression would come, you know. The young people ... how many people just married - they don't know how to cook, they don't know how to make bread; they'd have a time wouldn't they?

speaker: Connie Richard
words: I guess so; I was kind of lucky too! Because I, well, I was in the Peace Corps for a couple years in South American in a little rural village, you know, and I had to bake my own bread and learn how to cook things like you did, you know; had to buy things from the villiage market that weren't packaged and ...

speaker: Connie Richard
words: ... so I learned some of these things, but alot of young women don't know how to do that. And, I know how to sew; alot of girls don't know how to sew.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, you're lucky, you're lucky. That's all that a girl cared to.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, things are so different now.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: They have things at home that occupy their time, and they don't bother.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Do you think sometimes, sometimes when I talk to older women like you I get the feeling that you had such a, you felt like you had alot of meaning to your life, you know, when you were younger and as you grew older and everything?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I often think about it; I remember my first ... oh, that was a thrill, my first phonograph. My mother was in the hotel, I told you she run, and there was a fellow that come along with a phonograph and some-records and a big horn. And, of course, she told him he could have a portion of the dining room to have people come in. Well, I got ahold of a nickel and put it in, and the song wasn't appropriate for me - I only got a few notes, and away went my nickel! My mother .. , wouldn't let me listen to it. Yes, I remember my first phonograph .... remember my first moving picture.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Oh, tell me about that.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, it was nothing. It was a big boat, and people walking on the deck.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Did they have a movie-house or something where you saw it?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Where - in Troy?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Libby. Yeah, just walking around; free picture.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: It was a silent picture?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, but that was wonderful.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Must have been exciting to see something like that.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh, out of this world.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, did you have radio at that time?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: The motion picture came before radio, huh?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah. No, we didn't have no TV; nothing.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: I know you didn't have TV.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, I remember the first one I've seen was in Green Bay.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: A TV?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, it was New Year's and there was a tavern close by where we were staying with some of these people and, oh, the T.V. was there. And, they were serving a dinner and their main course was champagne-baked ham baked in champagne. Well, we went to eat some to see this television. Why, if a noise or a ear within a block would come - there it was. Like this, but we thought it was wonderful.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Tell me a story about your husband so that I can get a feeling for what kind of person he was.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, my husband, of course, came from a big family. And his father was the wholesale liquor dealer, in Green Bay. And, I've seen pictures of their home and they seemed to have everything. He was a very ... , I'm inclined to be a little bit outspoken, you know, in Jerry's story - and I always have fun. Well, he was very quiet; I don't know how he ever lived with me. And, honest. I'll tell you, when we lost him people came from miles, miles, miles; he had alot of friends. And, as I say, he was a quiet person. He left home and got out in the woods, and kind of pulled-back from his church.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Do you know why - did he ever say why?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yes, there were things he just couldn't figure out.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Like what?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, what really the meaning of these things are; what it means to him - and he wasn't a very good Catholic. Of course, I was a Protestant, which was never mentioned, never. And, I've always felt that maybe he left home a little early because the mother and the father, not the father so much, but the children seemed to stick to it better; I think he felt like he was a little outsider. And then, of course, he became a 'Mason'. And, I became a 'Star'. Well, he was very well thought of; very nice disposition, good to his family. We were talking the other night about punishing children. I don't ever think I've seen him strike one of them - to spank them. I did.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: I was going to ask you, "Did you?".

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, I would, but not him. He always said ... I'd say, "Oh, there's an awful bad kid." ... a mean kid or something ... he'd always say, "There is not such a thing as a bad child." Now I still think there is. Yeah, he was a very wonderful person; we had a very happy life.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, you know, there are alot of loggers now, they, well loggers kind of have the reputation that they drink alot and they, you know, go to houses of prostitution and things like that; now, your husband didn't...was it like that when he was a logger and he just didn't do that?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, I'll tell you, of course, I met him when I...he was ten years older than I, and he worked in the woods mostly for a while for my brother-in-law that was a logger, and I can remember him getting up a bunch of kids like me - my age, four or five and take us to a show, or take us someplace. But, no, he was always a good person. I know I was quite resentful about losing him; I couldn't understand why a person like him had to be taken so young - I thought seventy-two was young, but that time had come.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Have you resolved that in your mind now - do you feel better about it?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, yes.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: I guess you have to accept it.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: You have to, whether you want to or not. I feel so sorry here, for all of the people.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Why?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I mean, this is expensive - they haven't money; most of them, of course, get a Social Security check, and they get back a few dollars out of it, you know, $20 or something for personals. But, I know alot of them worry terribly, "Well, how will I pay it next month; what will happen next month?".

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Don't they get their check every month?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh, yes, Social Security.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: But, that's not enough?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: That's not enough! Well, my land; I, last month, mine was $534.00, and then it has run up to $600.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: If you need more medication or something?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, that medicine's terrible. Of course, I'm alright.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, can't you, can't they get Medicaid from the government or something?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, now, I don't think this place carries it; some of them don't - they don't help the good Samaritan, we don't get it. And my little jar, I've taken this medication - it's for bladder trouble, I don't take it all the time, but sometimes - about that high, about that much -enders, about $12.30.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, Myrtle, let me ask you a few more questions. I suppose that you, do you read magazines or watch, listen to the news or anything?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Listen, honey, I can't anymore on account of my eyes. Like yesterday, oh, I had these relatives from Canada, and she called me about a month ago and we had a long talk and the next day I wrote her a long letter. Well, then yesterday, a day before yesterday, came a letter from her says, "What on earth is happening?", says, "We haven't heard from you and we're worried and why don't you write?" Well, evidently, they didn't get that long letter that I wrote right after she called and they were worried. And, as I say, I don't; that writing yesterday ... now last night my eyes felt swollen, and they were red ... just from writing a letter, a long letter - I can't read! And, I don't watch alot of television - unless I don't look at it.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, what do you think ... it seems like women today are doing more, going more toward professional work, and they're having, alot of times they have their children taken care of in day-care centers and so on. That's alot different than the way you lived your life, and how do you feel about that?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I think it's wrong entirely.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: And, what are your reasons for that?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I think that there's a love - there's always - you have to have love, and there's no love like a mother's love; I think. A father might like them just as well, and all this kind of stuff, but a mother's love goes deep. I can never remember, it seems to me - unless she, my mother was out on a baby for somebody of coming home from school and not finding my mother! Now, some people are not too particular who they choose for a babysitter, and I feel that really rejection. I think a mother should take care of her children. Of course, there is a money part; but, by the time you pay a babysitter, you don't have alot left!

speaker: Connie Richard
words: What if a women is divorced or something and she doesn't have any way to have money?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, the welfare takes care of them.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: How do you feel about women being on welfare?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I've rented to quite alot of them. I know I rented to one woman, wasn't a very big house, but she had three little ones, and, it was sixty (Dollars) a month; I was always cheap on rent. And, she got to doing things that the neighbors didn't approve of - too many parties, too much drinking, and she always kicked , every time she paid that rent, she kicked ... although it was welfare. I thought, "Well, I'll raise your rent! And she'll leave!" So I raised the rent $15, and the next day they, Peter - a man from the welfare called me and he said, "Did you raise Francis' rent?", and I said, "Yes." Ha! That didn't work. No, I think there's too much of that give, give, give. Sometimes it's necessary, but alot of times it's not. I don't believe much in that welfare business.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Do you think life has changed alot for a woman now since you were younger?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, they live a different life. I often think of these girls, of course, I'm right there by the station, "Oh, I'm so tired, I am so tired, oh, I'm so tired!" But, after they get off work at 11 o'clock, alot of them, I know, they go out! And, they have families at home. I think there's been quite a change in living, in regards to the mother. I think a mother should go out once in a while or have a good time, and have the kids cared for, but not a steady diet - I don't believe in it. I never wanted to be away from my kids, I enjoyed the kids! What do you think? (Friend): I think that most mothers have benefitted from being with the kids, more and more. However, not all mothers were good mothers. You know that; there are some kids that don't have much of mothers, even those at home.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I'm sorry for them. Well, I was always quite a hand for children. I know when my sister married and had a little girl, and a fourteen month little boy, well, I raised those kids!

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Do you think that families used to help each other more than they do now?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yes.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: I wonder why they don't do that so much now?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I don't know, it seems to me like alot of selfishness. I really always did. I've done one thing in my life that I'm real proud of - I've taken care of five old people in my family. First my mother and father, of course, and then my sister, her husband, my husband.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Well, how do you feel then, would you like someone to take care of you now? Rather than be in here now?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I tried the idea of having steady help, but it didn't work out too good because, well, younger people, alot of younger people - I don't say all of them - were a nuisance. (Friend): Uh, part of it is she's always been so independent, I think, and able to cope in every way and it's difficult. It would be hard for me to stay with the family.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: My youngest boy has a big beautiful home; then he has just built a house - it's five miles from Edaville, up in the woods, timber. Well, he's built this house, it has a big living room, three bedrooms, and in back of the house, then, is a sauna bath, a barbaque room, a guest house, a wash room; it's a big thing.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: But, when you were younger, you say, you took care of older people - did you have them in your home?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: But you wouldn't want to live with any of them and have someone take care you.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, I don't want to live with any of them. (Friend): I understand that.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, they're good to me; my land. (Friend): I'm sure that Lois and Jim would just love to have you with them if you wanted to stay there. I'll vouche for that.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I know the little boy, he's thirteen, now he's the one that's leaving to night for Portland to take more swimming, and Jim's had him up the Antartic Circle fishing. They are very close, he and that boy. Now, he's come and talked with me the other day, he would tell me all about it. He said, "Well, I might take him to Denver - to be with the coach about ten days. I might," he says, "take a little run down." He said he might get lonesome; now that isn't it at all, they lie to me all the time. (Friend): Jim's getting lonesome!

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah. He's going to get lonesome with the kid! They lie to me all the time! I did almost have a nervous breakdown when he was sick; little hints here, there and ... now, I didn't cry - I'm not a crying woman, but I just went into shock like. And, one of the relatives called Lois and said, "Lois, I think you'd better come up and tell all about it." Early, early she came up. She said, "I've stopped in to talk with Jim a minute." I says, "Alright. And, she says, "I want to come look you in the eye and tell you the truth," she says, "I've lied so much." Well I said, "You're all liars!" But, she's a wonderful woman.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Myrtle, can you think of any other things that stick out in your mind when you were younger, or being older, a Christmas that you really liked, or a birthday, or a holiday?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I can remember, I kind of remembered my first Christmas. We were on the farm, in Farmington, and we went to a big house - nothing on the floor, just a bare floor and we were all getting sleepy. And, my mother said, "If you would just be still a little while, Santa Claus would come down the chimney." Well, I took that in; I went to sleep and fell and poked my head.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Oh, you bumped your head?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I never did see Santa Claus come down the chimney. Oh, I'll tell you, I always had a good time. (Friend): Keeps you young.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I always had a good time. Always.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Did you like the dresses you used to have to wear when you were younger - did you wear long dresses and high-top shoes?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, yes, because we didn't know any better. We were illiterate! But, of course, -as I say, my husband was ten years older than I and he always said, "Well, I fell in love with you when I first seen you.", and he would tell about the dress I had on. It was light-blue and white checks, and it had two ruffles, ha! ha! ha!, around the bottom, and ruffles here ... (Friend): And you mean way down at the bottom!

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yep. Well, we were very happy, you know, he was a good man. I don't know how he ever lived with me, really, because he was quiet and I'm not!

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Is there anything else you wanted to tell me?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: There was an old lady, I mean, she was married when I was just a young girl, and she liked me awfully well, and she hated to cook. And, I lived close and she would call me and ... "After you cook dinner - make a cake or make some pies or something, I'll make you a new dress! " And I always dressed well because this woman liked me - she had no girls. She ended up in .. out of Reno, close to Reno; she had a boy by her first husband, and then she remarried, again after he died, but this boy of hers he was in high school and he wanted to kill a wild horse. At that time they were making alot of, oh, different things out of horse-hair, and he wanted to go out and kill a wild horse to have the mane and the tail and so forth. Well, his step father had bought him a .22, and he was awfully proud to get to carry this gun, you know. So, in a couple of days they were in sheep country, as level as this floor, and there was a sheepherder came along and said, "How's my boy?" '.'Why, he said, "I haven't seen your boy." Well, he left for the camp two days ago or something; they said he never came. Well, they went out by the hundreds searching for him, you know ..

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Where was this Myrtle?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Close to Reno ..and, anyway, they hunted and hunted, and she lost her mind. And, they find her at night - get out of bed and go out to digging the sand, trying to find him. But, anyway, he was gone seven years when there was a big bunch of sheep came over this little mound that had been built, you know, by animals - I mean sheep - in order to cross them over, and there was his body; close to home ... close to home! So, of course, she just flipped. And, I went to Reno several times to visit her, we were awfully close - of course, she was alot older than I was. And, when she had her stroke, it was on her deathbed, ~· they sent for me and I went. But, the boy, the gun had exploded. So, I don't know, I think there is alot of difference in everything.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: When you were married, give me an idea of what a normal day would be like for you; what time you would get up and what you would do and so on.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, of course, I got up fairly early because he was in school - that's when he took this course in Missoula, and I was alone alot. I didn't know anybody. And, I was under the impression that I looked horrible.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Why?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well ... I thought I looked horrible, I didn't want strangers getting glaring at me. But we managed to get through what we had to take. On five dollars a week.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: So, you'd get up early and make breakfast?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh yes, I'd always cook.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Oh, yeah, what'd you have for breakfast?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I never, never was a breakfast eater. He wanted a good breakfast. Of course, he didn't always get it! When we was living on five dollars a week. , (Friend): What was his idea of a good breakfast? MB; Well, he liked pancakes, and, of course, we would always have either bacon or ham or sausage. Here I ... I forgot what a piece of bacon looks like.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You don't get bacon here?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I think we've had it twice. Oh, about a week ago I got hot and hopped on the administrator and he says, "All you have to do is just to re-order, and you'll get more." Well I said, "I've done it with bacon and I never got any." And I had it then. That was my first day here. I think I have it in one of those other records about my family. Of course, there were three children born in Oregon. They crossed the plains, of course, with everybody else, you know, in the old covered wagon and the oxen, ,and they landed in Eugene, Oregon. My father went to the Gold Rush in '49, and one of my mother's brothers went. My father, I know nothing about him, very little. He was born in England, and he had a nursemaid. And, she had him, I think he was about four months old, and she was coming here, and she brought him, and he never knew his parents - only that the father was a lawyer. And this woman finally married here in this country, and had children, but when he was about ...

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Why would his parents let him go away like that?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I don't know.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You don't think he might have been illegitimate or something?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: That's just what I often thought.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: I wonder; you know, he might be the son of a famous person like a Churchill or a Cornwallace or something.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yes. And anyway, she did tell him the right thing, so she said. Well, the family seemed to resent him a little bit. But, anyway, she was on her deathbed and she called him and she told him that she had brought him from England, and that these people were not his real parents. Well, of course then, he said they wasn't kind to him after that, so he run away and ended up with my mother's people in Missouri. And, then when they came here, of course they, he come with them and they settled around Eugene - they had three children there. He stayed though; he stayed in California in Balsam Acreage in what would now be the center of San Francisco. Of course, he was over there years ago. But, anyway, then they came out to Farmington, and there were six of us born there. But, my father was the first County Commissioner in Whitman County, and they had a, there was just a little ... I don't think it was much of a building, although it was big enough to have dances in, so they told me, my sister used to go there to dances. They finally moved down into Colfax and -built this suburb, a court house. But, he was the first County Commissioner in Whitman County.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Uh-huh. That reminds me of something I wanted to ask you about your life; what did you do for enjoyment - did you ever go to dances or things like that?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I never missed a -dance.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You like dancing, huh?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I never missed one.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Also ... did you do any other things besides dancing?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I used to be able to sing quite well. In fact, I have sang in the church choir. Now I don't even go to church! (Friend): Uh, it might be kind of nice if you described some the dances you went to; what kind of dances were they-were they in the schools or a get together for the family?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, that was the kind we used to have ... I'll tell you something, there was never, when I was a young teenager growing up, there was never a drunk person at a dance. Now, you can't have a good time unless you get drunk before you get there! Ha! Ha! Nope, we never had drinking.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: How did you meet your husband?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, he came out from Green Bay - a young man - and worked for my brother in-law.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Were you staying with your brother-in-law?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Alot of the time, yes ... because I liked those kids ... I wanted to be with the kids! Yeah!

speaker: Connie Richard
words: And you fell in love?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Fell in love; he was a wonderful person

speaker: Connie Richard
words: And, what was your courtship like; was it a long courtship?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, as I say, he had a wonderful disposition; I never did have a 'sweet' disposition. I don't know how he ever lived with me.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: What was courting like? What did you do for courting?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, go to dances, go to a show.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Did you have to have a chaperone or anything?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, I never did.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You two would go together?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah. Mostly there was a gang of us. I was telling the folks the other night, we were talking about, oh, the other kids around, and I said, "Well, I I remember the first time a boy kissed me, and they laughed, you know, hee, hee, hee', and I said, "It was the preacher's son." Ha! Ha! My first kiss from a boy was from the preachers son!

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Were you shocked?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: We were about fifteen, and it scared me to death! I thought, "Oh, my God! Kissed by a boy! Why, that's terrible!"

speaker: Connie Richard
words: And, you were how old when you got married then?

speaker: Connie Richard
words: So, you were a little older than alot of girls were too.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, I was an old maid.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Were you ... were you getting worried that you wouldn't get married?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, no, no. I knew when I got ready, I had one all picked out.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Okay, well, I think that we've covered most of the ...

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I was going to tell you, I slipped up a little bit, uh, when we moved from, well, not me - I wasn't born - but, when my family moved to Eugene, mother hadn't been living there long before she had a baby, a baby boy - Burneil, the last one. And, there was another baby born; they were born at the same time. And there was, though, there~was not many minutes between them, their birth - twin - that he was the first white child born in Whitman County; they are sure he was, but there were two of them. (Friend): Couldn't determine which!

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Yeah, and that there were few minutes.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: You mean, most of the population was Indian or what?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No. (Friend); It was raw land ... whites hadn't settled yet, see.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Oh, I see. (Friend): Old folks came, but the babies were either born on the way, or they set - on their way laters.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: You know, my mother has told ... ! was awfully close to my mother, about liquor. She said they all started out from Missouri with lots of liquor. They kind of used it for a medication, I guess. And, her grandfather died on the plain and she said, "When the liquor run out - he died!" (Friend): He had a week .. ha!

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, have I been any good to you?

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Oh, fantastic!

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, I'll tell you, if you can get that recording I made, and test , it; I was unprepared this time, or I would have looked up dates more acurately.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: We have a pretty good idea.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: But, if you want to. I know you could get, use that record that I made for the students in Coeur d'Alene, because it went to high schools and all. (Friend): You gave her the particulars on that, did you, she's the one ....

speaker: Connie Richard
words: I'm writing this up here-now, where would that tape be, do you know?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: In the library.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: In the library where?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: In Coeur d'Alene.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: The public library?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I don't know. (Friend): Maybe those people last night from Coeur d'Alene might locate it.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I don't know. Now, that was the one ... did you know Lizzy Kawski? (Friend): Yes.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, it was her son, graduating, that I made it for.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: And, you said there was another one at Moscow too?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: One in Moscow; how that's the one at the University~ I'm sure. Well, that was sponsored by the Retired Teachers; Scrappert. (Friend): Oh, Bud Scrappert.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: That might be ... there is another oral history project; Okay, what did you want to tell me now?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: The railroad that comes from Harrison, you know, goes on up the moss, that goes through some Indian reservation. And, when they started to build the road, of course they figured on buying the right of way, and, like you do, you know, and ... they said, "no! they didn't want any money", all they wanted was when they had to go someplace, they could go on the train free ... ha! ha! Yeah! The indians! Kinda funny.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Did you ever have any trouble with the Indians in your earlier days or anything?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: No, no.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: They've always been friendly?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I told you, didn't I earlier, didn't I tell you about Chief Joseph going on the rampage?

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Uh-uh.

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Well, now it would be about the time I was born, about 87 years ago; he went on the war-path and the people around that community, around Farmington, and they were afraid to have their families there. So they, everybody, loaded up their families and divided the ride in a wagon, and went to Colfax. I can't remember whether mother said they put us in a church or a schoolhouse, but there were lots of kids, and they both got rid of the measles. And, my father came, he got worried about if they had enough food and everything, and drove over to see what was going on.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Now, did you say you were little then? Or you weren't born?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: I. .. just a tiny baby. And, mother said, "No, I want to go home." She said, "I would rather fight Chief Joseph than live amongst these sick kids'.' So she went home, and she's never seen Chief Joseph.

speaker: Connie Richard
words: Now, is there anything else ...

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Oh, dear ...

speaker: Connie Richard
words: ... that you want to talk about?

speaker: Myrtle Bening
words: Not off hand ... really.
